claims.text: Overall HEA tribo-corrosion degradation is governed by coupling between wear-induced microstructural evolution and modification of the protective passive oxide film.
Mechanical wear exposes fresh, more reactive substrate.
Wear-induced microstructural changes modulate passive-film stability and repair.
The proposed initial material is a coarse-grained, single-phase, additively manufactured or heat-treated HEA.
The proposed initial material has an intact protective passive oxide film.
Sliding strain dynamically refines grains in the HEA surface layer.
Sliding produces localized amorphization in the HEA surface layer.
Wear-induced grain refinement and amorphization govern hardness, friction, and passive-film stability or thickness.
Formation of grain boundaries and amorphous regions disrupts the continuity of the passive oxide film.
Newly exposed or grain-refined regions can be more reactive and therefore accelerate corrosion.
Grain refinement can enhance repassivation kinetics in some regimes.
The net tribo-corrosion response reflects a balance between wear-driven passive-film breakdown and passive-film reformation on refined grains.
Tribo-corrosion will produce a higher overall degradation rate than corrosion without sliding.
Sliding in the corrosive medium will raise the corrosion current density relative to the corrosion-only baseline.
Wear rates will increase relative to the corrosion-only baseline.
The degradation response may vary nonlinearly with the extent of microstructural refinement and the repassivation capability.
Alloying, surface treatment, or formation of a stable dense microstructure may suppress the proposed degradation mechanism by improving tribo-corrosion resistance or repassivation.
The coupled response is sensitive to pH, electrolyte composition, and sliding conditions.
A comparison of composition- and microstructure-matched specimens in 3.5% NaCl, with and without sliding, can test the proposed coupling.

The hypothesis is falsified if sliding causes no significant grain refinement, passive-film degradation, or electrochemical increase, or if total degradation is only the additive sum of independent wear and corrosion contributions.
